meta.blurb: In 1860 Abraham Lincoln beat three famous rivals for his party's nomination, then did something astonishing: he asked them to help him run the country in its darkest hour. Meet the proud, brilliant men around the table.
meta.bible: Abraham Lincoln: 16th president of the United States, born 1809 in a Kentucky log cabin, self-taught lawyer of Springfield, Illinois, elected 1860, re-elected 1864, shot 14 April 1865 and died the next morning. Mary Todd Lincoln: his wife. Willie Lincoln: their son, died February 1862 aged eleven. William Seward: senator and former governor of New York, favourite for the 1860 nomination, became Secretary of State, stayed on until 1869, bought Alaska from Russia in 1867. Salmon Chase: senator and governor of Ohio, Secretary of the Treasury 1861 to June 1864, then Chief Justice from December 1864. Edward Bates: older Missouri lawyer, Attorney General until November 1864, kept a diary. Simon Cameron: Pennsylvania political boss, first Secretary of War, left in January 1862. Edwin Stanton: lawyer, took over the War Department in January 1862, a hard worker. Gideon Welles: Connecticut newspaper editor, Secretary of the Navy for the whole war, kept a diary. Montgomery Blair: Postmaster General, resigned September 1864. Caleb Smith: Secretary of the Interior. Stephen Douglas: Illinois senator, Lincoln's opponent in the 1858 debates and in 1860. David Davis: Lincoln's friend, a judge, who led his convention team. George McClellan: general, replaced November 1862, Lincoln's opponent in 1864. Robert E Lee: Confederate general. Ulysses Grant: Union general. Jefferson Davis: president of the Confederacy. John Wilkes Booth: the actor who shot Lincoln. Places and events: Springfield, Chicago and its Wigwam hall (convention May 1860, Lincoln won on the third ballot), Cooper Union in New York (February 1860), Fort Sumter in Charleston harbour (attacked 12 April 1861), Antietam (September 1862), Gettysburg (July 1863, speech November 1863), Atlanta (fell September 1864), Appomattox (9 April 1865), Ford's Theatre. Emancipation Proclamation: preliminary 22 September 1862, signed 1 January 1863, covered areas in rebellion. Thirteenth Amendment: passed Congress January 1865, ended slavery. Voice and tone: clear, warm and fair, a true story told step by step; deaths are stated plainly with no gore; where historians disagree it is said so; numbers are given as about.

B1B2: In 1860 the United States was close to breaking apart, mostly because of slavery. A new party called the Republicans wanted to choose a president who could win.
Abraham Lincoln was born in 1809 in a log cabin in Kentucky, to a poor farming family. He had very little time in school, so he taught himself by reading whatever books he could borrow.
Lincoln became a lawyer in Springfield, Illinois, and travelled from town to town to argue cases. People trusted him for his honesty, and he served one term in Congress in the late 1840s.
In 1858 Lincoln ran for the Senate against Stephen Douglas, and the two men held seven public debates about slavery. Lincoln lost the election, but newspapers carried his words far beyond Illinois.

In February 1860 Lincoln travelled to New York to speak at a college hall called Cooper Union. He argued carefully that the nation's founders had wanted to limit slavery, and the audience was deeply impressed.
William Seward had been governor of New York and was now a senator, and he was the most famous man in the new party. Many people thought the nomination was his, and Seward thought so too.
Salmon Chase had been a senator and was then the governor of Ohio. He was proud, serious and hard-working, and he believed that he should be president.

Edward Bates was an older lawyer from Missouri, a slave state, and many thought him calm and careful. Simon Cameron was a powerful politician from Pennsylvania, and his supporters were ready to bargain.
In May 1860 the Republicans met in Chicago, in a huge new wooden hall called the Wigwam. Thousands of people crowded in to watch, and the noise was tremendous.
On the first ballot Seward received the most votes, but he was well short of the number he needed. Lincoln came in second, which surprised many people in the hall.

Lincoln's friends told delegates that he could win the states the party needed, and that he had made fewer enemies than Seward. Many delegates liked the idea, because the Republicans wanted above all to win in November.
In Springfield, Lincoln waited for news to arrive by telegraph from Chicago. Historians still disagree about what promises, if any, his friends made to win votes for him.
On the third ballot, delegate after delegate switched to Lincoln, and he won the nomination. Seward, who had been so sure of victory, was deeply disappointed.
Seward was deeply hurt, but he did not sulk or complain about the result. That autumn he travelled across the country making speeches for Lincoln, and Chase also spoke for the party in Ohio.
Four men ran for president in 1860, and the vote was split among them. Lincoln won with fewer than half of the votes, and his name was not on the ballot in most Southern states.

South Carolina left the Union in December 1860, and six more Southern states soon followed it. Together they formed a new government, the Confederate States of America, and chose Jefferson Davis as its president.
In Springfield, Lincoln began to choose the men who would advise him in his cabinet. To everyone's surprise, he decided to ask the very men who had run against him.
Lincoln offered Seward the most important job in the cabinet, Secretary of State. Seward hesitated and even changed his mind once, but in the end he agreed to serve.

Salmon Chase became head of the Treasury, and Edward Bates became Attorney General. Simon Cameron, Gideon Welles, Caleb Smith and Montgomery Blair received other posts, so the cabinet had seven members.

In March 1861 Lincoln took the oath of office outside the Capitol, whose great dome was still unfinished. In his speech he told Southerners that they were friends, not enemies, and that he did not want a war.
At first, Seward behaved as if he were the real leader of the government. He had much more experience than Lincoln, and he saw himself as the man who would guide the new president.

When Seward suggested that someone else might take charge of policy, Lincoln replied politely but firmly that the decisions were his. Seward accepted this, and from then on the two men worked together closely.

Fort Sumter, a Union fort in the harbour of Charleston, South Carolina, was running short of food. Lincoln's cabinet disagreed about what to do, and he had to decide how to help the soldiers without starting a war.

Before dawn on 12 April 1861, Confederate guns opened fire on Fort Sumter, and the fort surrendered after about a day. Lincoln called for seventy-five thousand volunteers to defend the Union, and four more Southern states then left it.
In cabinet meetings Lincoln let strong men argue openly, and he listened carefully to each side. When the talk was over, he made the decision himself, and he did not simply follow the majority.
Chase had to find enormous sums of money to pay for the war. He sold government bonds to ordinary people and agreed to a new paper money, which people called greenbacks.
Gideon Welles, a newspaper editor from Connecticut, had to make the navy much bigger very quickly. His ships blocked Southern ports, so the Confederacy found it harder to sell cotton and buy weapons.

Edward Bates gave the president careful legal advice and wrote down his thoughts in a private diary. Montgomery Blair, as Postmaster General, worked to improve the mail, which mattered a great deal to soldiers far from home.

Early in 1862 Simon Cameron left the War Department after complaints about waste and bad contracts. Lincoln chose Edwin Stanton to replace him, even though Stanton had criticised him in earlier years.
General George McClellan trained a huge army well, but he was always slow to attack. Lincoln and Stanton lost patience with him, and Lincoln finally replaced him in November 1862.
In February 1862 Lincoln's eleven-year-old son Willie died of a fever in the White House. Lincoln and his wife Mary grieved deeply, yet the war would not wait, and he went back to work.
In July 1862 Lincoln read his cabinet a draft order that would free the slaves in the states fighting against the Union. He had already made up his mind, but he asked for their advice.
Seward warned that the order might look like a cry of desperation if it came after a defeat. He advised waiting for a military victory, and Lincoln, after thinking, put the paper away.

In September 1862 Union soldiers stopped General Lee's army at Antietam, in the bloodiest single day in American history. Days later Lincoln announced that on New Year's Day the slaves in the rebel states would be free.
On New Year's Day 1863 Lincoln signed the Emancipation Proclamation. It did not free everyone at once, because it applied only to areas in rebellion, but it changed what the war was about.
After the proclamation, Black men were welcomed into the Union army and navy. Before the war ended, close to two hundred thousand of them had served, and they helped to win it.

In the first days of July 1863, the Union army stopped General Lee at Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, after three days of terrible fighting. Many thousands of men died, and Lee's army had to retreat to Virginia.

In November 1863, Lincoln went to Gettysburg to open a new cemetery for the soldiers who had died. His speech lasted only a few minutes, but it asked the nation to finish the work for which they had died.

As 1864 began, some of Chase's supporters wrote a letter saying that he would make a better president than Lincoln. When it became public, Chase was embarrassed, but Lincoln stayed calm and did not dismiss him at once.
After another quarrel, this time about who should hold a Treasury post in New York, Chase offered to resign. He had done so before, but this time, in June 1864, Lincoln accepted.
Montgomery Blair resigned in September 1864, partly because other Republicans disliked him. Edward Bates left later that autumn, and Lincoln chose new men to take their places.
In the summer of 1864 the war dragged on, and Lincoln feared that he would lose the election. Then the army captured Atlanta, and in November the voters chose him again by a large margin.
When the old chief justice died in 1864, Lincoln chose Salmon Chase to take his place. Chase had caused him much trouble, but he also knew that Chase firmly opposed slavery.

Lincoln and Seward worked hard to win the last votes for the Thirteenth Amendment, which would end slavery across the whole country. It passed the House in January 1865, and the states approved it later that year.

In his second inaugural speech in March 1865, Lincoln spoke of finishing the war with “malice toward none” and “charity for all”. He asked the nation to bind up its wounds and care for those who had suffered.

On the ninth of April 1865 General Lee surrendered his army to General Grant at Appomattox, and the fighting began to end. A few days earlier, Seward had been badly hurt in a carriage accident and was lying in bed at home.
On the night of 14 April 1865, Lincoln went to Ford's Theatre in Washington to see a play. There an actor named John Wilkes Booth shot him, and the president died the next morning.

That same night, a man forced his way into Seward's house and attacked him as he lay in bed. Seward was badly wounded, but he lived, and the metal brace on his broken jaw is thought to have helped save his life.
At Lincoln's bedside, Stanton, once a critic, wept openly, and Welles and others mourned too. Seward recovered, stayed in office under the next president, and bought Alaska from Russia in 1867.
Lincoln did not fear men who were proud or clever, and he turned former rivals into valuable helpers. His story shows that a good leader can learn a great deal from people who disagree.
C1C2: In the spring of 1860 the United States was a nation arguing with itself, and the argument was about slavery, which many Northern states had abolished and which the South was determined to keep. A young political party, the Republicans, believed that slavery should not be allowed to spread into new lands. Its members were about to meet in Chicago to choose a man who could carry that belief into the White House, and the most famous candidates were not the one they finally chose.

Abraham Lincoln was born in 1809 in a one-room log cabin in Kentucky, and his family later moved north, first to Indiana and then to Illinois, in search of better land. He attended school for only a short time, yet he became a hungry reader who borrowed any book within walking distance. The habit of patient study, learned in those lonely years, would later shape the way he understood both law and people.

Lincoln taught himself the law, moved to Springfield, Illinois, and spent years riding from one country courthouse to the next, arguing cases for farmers, merchants and railway companies. His skill with words was matched by a reputation for honesty that clung to him long before he was famous. After one quiet term in Congress in the late 1840s, he went home to his law practice, and he seemed to have left politics behind.

In 1858 Lincoln challenged the famous senator Stephen Douglas to a series of seven open-air debates, in which the two men argued fiercely over whether slavery should be allowed to spread. Douglas kept his Senate seat, because in those days the state legislature chose the senator. Yet the printed speeches travelled far beyond Illinois, and the tall lawyer who had lost the contest was suddenly a name that Republicans across the North knew.

In February 1860 Lincoln travelled east to speak at Cooper Union in New York, where an audience that did not know him well heard a carefully reasoned argument instead of a country lawyer's jokes. He showed, with long and patient evidence, that the nation's founders had believed the federal government could limit slavery in the territories. The speech was printed in newspapers and made many Eastern Republicans think of him as a serious candidate.

William Seward had been governor of New York and was a senator of long experience, a clever, witty man whose speeches against slavery had made him the best known Republican in the country. He had worked for years to prepare for this moment and plainly expected the nomination to come to him. But his strong words had also made enemies, and some party leaders feared that he could never win the states that the Republicans needed.

Salmon Chase of Ohio had served as a senator and as governor, and he was known for his firm and lifelong opposition to slavery. Tall, serious and deeply sure of his own abilities, he longed for the presidency and had quietly worked toward it for years. In 1860 he found that even his own state was not fully united behind him.

Edward Bates, a respected lawyer from Missouri, offered a calm and conservative image that might appeal to voters in the border states. Simon Cameron of Pennsylvania was a shrewd political boss who controlled many votes and who was ready to bargain for them. Neither man was likely to win outright, but each could help to decide who did.

In May 1860 the Republican delegates gathered in Chicago, in a huge, newly built wooden hall that people called the Wigwam. Thousands of spectators crowded the galleries, cheering and shouting for their favourites, and at times the noise was so great that the speakers could barely be heard. Lincoln himself stayed at home in Springfield, and his friends did the work of winning delegates.

When the first ballot was counted, Seward led with about a hundred and seventy votes, which was impressive but still well short of the two hundred and thirty-three that he needed to win. Lincoln, who was far less famous, came second, and Chase, Bates and Cameron trailed some distance behind him. The hall was suddenly full of whispering, because a second ballot would reveal whether Seward's strength was real.

Lincoln's managers, led by his friend and fellow lawyer David Davis, spent the days before the vote persuading delegates that their man was everyone's second choice and nobody's enemy. They argued that he could carry the swing states of the North that Seward might lose. It was a practical argument, and it proved more powerful than any speech about greatness.

Back in Springfield, Lincoln waited calmly for the telegraph to bring news from Chicago, knowing that his friends were bargaining on his behalf. Historians still disagree about exactly what promises were made to the delegations of Pennsylvania and other states, and about how much Lincoln knew. What is clear is that some of those who helped him would later be rewarded.

On the third ballot the delegates began to shift toward Lincoln in large numbers, and when the last votes were counted the lawyer from Illinois had won the nomination. The roar of the crowd carried far across the city, and in Springfield, a crowd gathered to congratulate him. For Seward, who had waited for this honour for so long, the defeat was a bitter and public humiliation.

Seward was hurt, yet he swallowed his disappointment and set out that autumn on a long speaking tour, urging crowds across the North to vote for the man who had beaten him. Chase also spoke for the party in Ohio, and Bates gave his support more quietly. Their loyalty, whatever it cost them privately, showed that these proud men were willing to put the party's cause first, at least in public.

Four candidates competed in the election of November 1860, and the opposition to Lincoln was divided among three of them, so that he won the presidency with a little under forty per cent of the popular vote. His name did not even appear on the ballot in most of the Southern states, where he was widely feared as an enemy. Yet the Northern states gave him the electoral votes he needed, and a man who had lost a Senate race two years earlier was now president-elect.

Within weeks of Lincoln's election, South Carolina announced that it was leaving the Union, and by early February 1861 six more Southern states had followed it. Together they formed the Confederate States of America and chose Jefferson Davis as their president, while the outgoing government in Washington did little to stop them. Lincoln, who would not take office until March, had to watch the country break apart without any power to prevent it.

In his small office in Springfield, Lincoln began to choose the cabinet, the group of department heads who would help him run the government. He did something that few leaders would have dared to do, which was to invite his strongest rivals into the room. His reasons seem to have been partly political, because he needed the support of their followers, and partly practical, because he thought they were simply the ablest men available.

Lincoln offered Seward the most important position in the cabinet, that of Secretary of State, and after some thought Seward accepted. Even so, he wavered at the last moment, wondering whether he really wanted to serve under a man he considered less experienced than himself. A polite and firm letter from Lincoln settled the matter, and Seward agreed to join the government.

Chase was entrusted with the Treasury, whose coffers would soon have to fund a conflict that few yet imagined, and Bates became Attorney General, the government's chief legal adviser. Simon Cameron assumed command of the War Department, Gideon Welles the Navy, Caleb Smith the Interior, and Montgomery Blair the Post Office. The ministers came from different states and divergent political backgrounds, and several of them had little reason to cherish one another or the president himself.

In March 1861 Lincoln took the oath of office on the east side of the Capitol, where the great dome stood unfinished beneath its cranes like a symbol of the unfinished nation. His inaugural address was firm about keeping the Union together but tender toward the South, for he reminded his countrymen that they were not enemies but friends. Many Southerners were not listening, and the new president knew that his words might be the last chance for peace.

In the first weeks, Seward behaved as if he were the real head of the government and Lincoln merely its figurehead. He had spent decades in public life and had met everyone of importance, while the new president had spent two years in Congress and had never run anything larger than a law office. Seward's confidence was not entirely absurd, but it was about to meet a patient and stubborn man.

In early April Seward sent the president a note that hinted that someone besides Lincoln should direct policy, and a less secure man might have been offended. Instead Lincoln wrote a calm, courteous reply, saying that if any policy was to be followed it would be his own. Seward understood the message, and over the following months his respect for Lincoln deepened into a close and loyal friendship.

Fort Sumter, a small Union fort on an island in the harbour of Charleston, South Carolina, was surrounded by Confederate guns and was running short of food. Some of the cabinet urged Lincoln to give up the fort, while others wanted to send supplies, and each side had good reasons. He chose to send food but not weapons, so that if the shooting started, it would be the South that fired the first shot.

Before dawn on 12 April 1861, Confederate guns opened fire on Fort Sumter, and after about a day of bombardment the little garrison surrendered. Lincoln responded by calling for seventy-five thousand volunteers to defend the Union, and the North answered with a wave of eager recruits. But four more Southern states, among them the powerful state of Virginia, chose that moment to leave, and the long war began in earnest.

In the cabinet room, Lincoln let his strong-minded ministers argue freely, and he seemed to learn more from their disagreements than he would have from flattery. He listened carefully, asked shrewd questions and often told a story to ease the tension, but in the end the decision was always his own. Some of the men found this maddening, yet most of them came to respect a leader who could hear them out without losing his way.

As Secretary of the Treasury, Chase faced the grim task of paying for a war that cost more every month than the government had ever spent in a year. He sold bonds to banks and to ordinary citizens, and he accepted, with some reluctance, a new paper money that people called greenbacks. His financial measures were not perfect, but they kept the Union army fed, armed and paid, and that was no small achievement.

Gideon Welles, a newspaper editor from Connecticut with a long white beard, was given the job of enlarging a small navy at great speed. He bought, built and borrowed hundreds of ships, and they formed a blockade along the Southern coast that made it harder for the Confederacy to sell its cotton and import weapons. His diary, kept faithfully throughout the war, is now one of the best sources for what the cabinet said and did.

Edward Bates, the Attorney General, was a cautious man who gave the president careful legal advice and recorded his private doubts in a diary that historians still read with profit. Montgomery Blair, the Postmaster General, came from a well-connected political family and worked to make the mail faster and more reliable. A letter from home could be worth more to a homesick soldier than a ration of food, and Blair seems to have understood it.

Early in 1862, after complaints that the War Department was wasteful and badly managed, Simon Cameron left the cabinet, and Lincoln replaced him with the lawyer Edwin Stanton. Stanton had criticised Lincoln in earlier years, and some people were astonished that the president would trust him with so vital a task. But Stanton worked extremely long hours, organised the department with ferocious energy, and became one of the president's most valuable and most loyal supporters.

General George McClellan was a brilliant organiser who built a huge and well-trained army, but he was always convinced that the enemy was stronger than it really was. Lincoln and Stanton pleaded, coaxed and finally lost patience, and the president removed him from command in November 1862. The search for a general who would fight as boldly as Lincoln wished lasted for years and cost a great many lives.

In February 1862 Lincoln's beloved eleven-year-old son Willie died of a fever in the White House, and both the president and his wife Mary were crushed by the loss. Lincoln found it difficult to speak of his son for a long time, yet the war would not wait, and the country's leader had to carry his sorrow into the cabinet room. Those who worked with him noticed that his grief made him quieter and more thoughtful, though not weaker.

In July 1862 Lincoln read his cabinet a draft of an order that would free the slaves in every state that remained in rebellion against the Union. He told the startled ministers that he had already decided to act, and that he wanted advice only about the details and the timing. The room filled with different opinions, and each of the rivals reacted in the way that his own character demanded.

Seward, with his usual political shrewdness, warned that an order issued after a string of defeats might look like the last desperate cry of a failing government. He advised the president to wait for a military victory so that the proclamation would seem to come from strength. Lincoln was struck by the argument, put the draft away in a drawer, and waited for the right moment.

On a single day in September 1862, Union and Confederate armies fought each other at Antietam in the bloodiest battle in American history, and when Lee's army withdrew, Lincoln saw his chance. A few days later he issued a preliminary proclamation, warning that on New Year's Day every slave in a state still in rebellion would be declared free. The cabinet's long debate had borne fruit, and the war's purpose was about to change.

On New Year's Day 1863 Lincoln signed the Emancipation Proclamation, which declared free all the slaves in the areas that were still in rebellion. It did not touch slavery in the loyal border states, and in the Confederacy it could be enforced only as the Union army advanced. Even so, it changed the meaning of the war, for from that day a Union victory would mean the end of slavery.

After the proclamation, the Union army began to enlist Black soldiers in large numbers, and free Black men from the North and men who had escaped slavery from the South joined the ranks together. By the end of the war close to two hundred thousand Black men had served in the army and navy, and they fought bravely in many battles. Lincoln, who had once hesitated over the idea, later said that their service had been of great value to the Union.

For three days in early July 1863, the armies of Lee and the Union general George Meade fought at Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, in the bloodiest battle ever fought in North America. When it ended, tens of thousands of men lay dead or wounded, and Lee's battered army was forced to withdraw to Virginia. The North had won a victory that many historians regard as the turning point of the war.

In November 1863, Lincoln travelled to Gettysburg to dedicate a cemetery for the soldiers who had fallen there, and some members of his cabinet went with him. The main speaker talked for two hours, but the president spoke for only a few minutes, saying that the nation had been born in liberty and must have a new birth of freedom. Hardly anyone in the crowd realised at that moment that they had heard one of the great speeches in history.

As the election year of 1864 began, some of Chase's friends circulated a letter praising him as a better candidate for president than Lincoln, and when it reached the newspapers, the Treasury Secretary was deeply embarrassed. Lincoln, who knew perfectly well what Chase's ambitions were, did not rage or dismiss him but let the matter fade. The supporters' plan collapsed, because most Republicans simply wanted the man who had led them through the war.

After yet another quarrel, this one about who should fill a Treasury post in New York, Chase once more offered to resign, as he had done several times before. This time, in June 1864, Lincoln surprised him by accepting, perhaps because he had grown weary of the pressure. The president could no longer put up with a minister who threatened to leave whenever he did not get his way.

Montgomery Blair resigned in September 1864 at the president's request, partly because many Republicans disliked him and wished him gone before the election. Edward Bates left in the autumn as well, and Lincoln picked new men to fill both places. Seward and Welles, however, remained, and the president still had around him some of the strong-willed advisers who had shared his first difficult years.

During the summer of 1864 the war seemed to have no end, the casualty lists lengthened, and Lincoln came to believe that he might lose the election to General McClellan. Then Union forces captured the great Southern city of Atlanta in September, and the mood of the Northern public suddenly improved. In November the voters gave Lincoln a decisive victory, and a clear majority of the soldiers who voted chose the man who had sent them to war.

When the elderly Chief Justice Roger Taney died in the autumn of 1864, Lincoln nominated Salmon Chase to take his place, and the Senate approved the choice on the same day. Chase had caused him a great deal of trouble, and the president had not forgotten it, but he also knew that Chase's opposition to slavery was sincere and unshakable. It was a generous choice, and it shows how much Lincoln valued ability over personal loyalty.

Lincoln believed that the Emancipation Proclamation, resting on the president's war powers, might be questioned after the war, and so he pressed Congress to pass an amendment to the Constitution. He and Seward worked hard to win the last votes needed in the House, and the Thirteenth Amendment passed in January 1865. The states approved it in December of that year, and slavery was abolished throughout the United States.

In his second inaugural address in March 1865, with victory in sight, Lincoln did not boast but spoke solemnly about the suffering that the war had caused to both sides. He asked his countrymen to finish the work with “malice toward none” and “charity for all”, and to bind up the nation's wounds. It was a speech about mercy, delivered by a man whose own rivals had learned to rely on his generosity.

On the ninth of April 1865, General Lee surrendered his army to General Ulysses Grant in a farmhouse at Appomattox Court House, and the great war began to end at last. Only days earlier, Seward had been thrown from his carriage in an accident that broke his jaw and arm, and he was now lying in bed at home. The news from Appomattox was a welcome tonic for the injured Secretary of State.

On the evening of 14 April 1865, Lincoln and his wife went to Ford's Theatre in Washington to watch a comedy, hoping for a few hours of peace. During the play an actor named John Wilkes Booth entered the president's box and shot him in the head, and Lincoln was carried to a house across the street. He died early the next morning, and a stunned nation learned that the man who had saved the Union was gone.

That same night, as part of the same conspiracy, a man forced his way into Seward's house and attacked the injured Secretary of State as he lay in bed. Seward and several others were wounded, but all of them survived, and the brace that held Seward's broken jaw is thought to have helped to save his life. For days the family kept the terrible news of Lincoln's death from him, so that he would not suffer a relapse.

At Lincoln's bedside, Edwin Stanton, who had once spoken of him with contempt, wept openly, and Gideon Welles and others in the room shared his grief. Seward recovered and stayed on under the next president, and in 1867 he arranged the purchase of Alaska from Russia, while Chase, as Chief Justice, later presided over the trial of President Andrew Johnson in the Senate. The men who had once competed with Lincoln had become part of the story that was now history.

Lincoln did not fear men who were proud, clever or ambitious, and he turned his former rivals into some of the most valuable servants the Union ever had. They were not always loyal, and they often disagreed, yet the arguments in his cabinet room sharpened his judgement and kept him from error. The story is not a fairy tale about perfect harmony, but a lasting lesson that strong leaders gain more from honest disagreement than from comfortable agreement.
